deep.reconstruction:
Context (from fol. 104r): we are on an algebraic curve f(x,y)=0 of genus rho. Riemann has fixed three kinds of algebraic differentials, all of the form G(x,y)/f'(x,y)·dx with f' = ∂f/∂y:
(i) phi_1,…,phi_rho: integrands of the first kind, ∫phi_alpha dx = omega(x,y)_alpha.
(ii) psi_1,…,psi_rho: integrands of the second kind, whose local expansions have no term of degree −1, so no residues. ∫psi_alpha dx = varpi(x,y)_alpha.
(iii) phi(x,y,xi,eta): an integrand of the third kind with a simple pole of residue 1 at the point (xi,eta). Its compensating residue sits at a fixed normalising point. ∫phi(x,y,xi,eta) dx = Omega(x,y,xi,eta).
These satisfy the 'interchange of argument and parameter' relation
∂/∂xi phi(x,y,xi,eta) − ∂/∂x phi(xi,eta,x,y) = Σ_alpha [phi_alpha(x,y) psi_alpha(xi,eta) − phi_alpha(xi,eta) psi_alpha(x,y)].

This page states the consequence, a normal-form or decomposition theorem.

THEOREM. For any rational F(x,y) on the curve,
∫F(x,y)dx = 𝔣(x,y) + Σ_i C_i Omega(x,y,xi_i,eta_i) + Σ_{alpha=1}^{rho} c_alpha omega(x,y)_alpha + Σ_{alpha=1}^{rho} c_{rho+alpha} varpi(x,y)_alpha,
with 𝔣 rational and C_i, c_k constants. The representation is unique.

Implicit argument (mine, standard):
1. Let (xi_i,eta_i) be the poles of F dx with nonzero residue, and take C_i = Res_{(xi_i,eta_i)} F dx. Then F − Σ C_i phi(x,y,xi_i,eta_i) has zero residue everywhere except possibly at the normalising point. The residue theorem forces it to vanish there too.
2. This leaves a differential of the second kind. At each pole, subtract derivatives of rational functions, for which the interchange relation supplies explicit candidates (e.g. ∂^k/∂xi^k of phi). This reduces it to a combination of the 2rho classes phi_alpha, psi_alpha.
3. The space of second-kind differentials modulo exact ones has dimension 2rho, i.e. H^1_dR(curve). Hence the c_k and the C_i are unique, and 𝔣 is unique up to an additive constant.

The struck line '+ c_1 phi(x,y)' is a false start, replaced by the omega terms.

Faint pencil (apparently on this side, under the bleed-through from the verso): log G(x,y) = [Σ ±]Omega(x,y,x_1,y_1) + … − eps_1 omega(x,y)_1 − eps_2 omega(x,y)_2 − ….
This applies the theorem to F = d log G/dx for a rational function G. The rational part vanishes, the C_i are the orders (±1) at the zeros and poles x_i of G, and only first-kind terms remain with constants eps_alpha. Equivalently, this is Abel's theorem written through normalised third-kind integrals.

The faint mirrored formulas lower on the sheet are show-through from 104r: ∫phi_alpha dx = omega_alpha, ∫psi_alpha dx = varpi_alpha, ∫phi(x,y,xi,eta)dx = Omega. So is the top-right G/f' = C_1 phi_1 + ….
errors: No mathematical error in the stated theorem.

Uniqueness holds only with the stated normalisations: 𝔣 is unique up to an additive constant, and Omega must have its second pole at a fixed point so that the C_i are just the residues. This is left implicit.
The first constant is written as a blotted 𝔈_1/𝔆_1, but the list of constants afterwards reads C_1, C_2, …; this is a notational slip.

In the pencil formula, the absence of varpi terms in the expansion of log G is correct only because d log G has no second-kind part. Strictly, the coefficients eps_alpha are not arbitrary but are sums of psi-integrals between zeros and poles. The pencil is too faint to see whether Riemann specified this.

results.what: Unique decomposition of an arbitrary abelian integral ∫F(x,y)dx into a rational part, normalised third-kind integrals Omega(x,y,xi_i,eta_i), and 2rho integrals of the first kind (omega_alpha) and second kind (varpi_alpha)
results.modern_name: Normal form of abelian integrals; H^1_dR of a curve has dimension 2g (first and second kind integrals spanning de Rham cohomology)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen, 1857, transcendental/surface form); Weierstrass for the algebraic formulation with explicit rational integrands H, H_alpha, H'_alpha (Crelle 52, 1856, hyperelliptic case; Berlin lectures 1860s–1875 general case)

results.what: Formulation via a third-kind integrand phi(x,y,xi,eta) obeying the interchange relation (from the previous page), used to reduce everything to 2rho basic integrals
results.modern_name: Weierstrass's 'Vertauschung von Argument und Parameter' / algebraic construction of normalised elementary integrals (fundamental bidifferential precursor)
results.usually_credited_to: Weierstrass (lectures on abelian functions, published in Werke vol. 4)

results.what: Pencil: log of a rational function expressed as a sum of third-kind integrals over its zeros and poles minus first-kind integrals
results.modern_name: Abel's theorem (form with normalised third-kind integrals)

deep.surprise_reason: The decomposition theorem itself is classical and in substance in Riemann 1857. What is mildly notable is that Riemann here works purely algebraically, with integrands G/f' and an explicit third-kind integrand satisfying the interchange relation. This is the formalism normally associated with Weierstrass's lectures. Whether these are Riemann's own developments or notes on Weierstrass's 1856 hyperelliptic work is unclear.
